Title: Lung cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Since tobacco smoking is the cause in vast majority of cases, the incidence of lung cancer is expected to rise in those countries with high or rising incidence of tobacco smoking. Even though populations at risk of developing lung cancer are easily identified, mass screening for lung cancer is not supported by currently available evidence. In the case of non-small cell lung cancer, a cure may be possible with surgical resection followed by post-operative chemotherapy in those diagnosed at an early stage. A small minority of patients who present with locally advanced disease may also benefit from pre-operative chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy to down stage the tumor to render it potentially operable. In a vast majority of patients, however, lung cancer presents at an advanced stage and a cure is not possible with currently available therapeutic strategies. Similarly, small cell lung cancer confined to one hemi-thorax may be curable with a combination of chemotherapy and thoracic irradiation followed by prophylactic cranial irradiation, if complete remission is achieved at the primary site. Small cell lung cancer that is spread beyond the confines of one hemi-thorax is, however, considered incurable. In this era of molecular targeted therapies, new agents are constantly undergoing pre-clinical and clinical testing with the aim of targeting the molecular pathways thought be involved in etiology and pathogenesis of lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This research is about lung cancer, which is the top cause of death from cancer (Abstract, sentence 1). It looks at how we treat lung cancer now, and why we still need better care (Abstract, sentence 6). This work may help people who smoke or used to smoke, and people who may get or already have lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). The team looked at how often lung cancer is found late, and what kinds of treatment can still help (Abstract, sentence 6). They also looked at when surgery, drug care, and beam care can lead to a cure in some people (Abstract, sentence 4). They found that most lung cancer is linked to smoking, and rates may rise where more people smoke (Abstract, sentence 2). They saw that wide use of scan tests to find lung cancer early is not yet backed by proof (Abstract, sentence 3). They found that some people with early non small cell lung cancer can be cured with surgery and drug care, and a few with more local disease may gain from drug care or beam care before surgery (Abstract, sentence 4). A small group with early small cell lung cancer can be cured with drug care and beam care, but once it has spread far, cure is not likely (Abstract, sentence 7). The study notes that many new “target” drugs are now in tests to block key cancer paths (Abstract, sentence 9). These may one day give more choices for people with lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 9).

Title: Lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: From a clinical perspective.
Abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and lung cancer are devastating pulmonary diseases that commonly coexist and present a number of clinical challenges. COPD confers a higher risk for lung cancer development, but available chemopreventive measures remain rudimentary. Current studies have shown a marked benefit of cancer screening in the COPD population, although challenges remain, including the common underdiagnosis of COPD. COPD-associated lung cancer presents distinct clinical features. Treatment for lung cancer coexisting with COPD is challenging as COPD may increase postoperative morbidities and decrease survival. In this review, we outline current progress in the understanding of the clinical association between COPD and lung cancer, and suggest possible cancer prevention strategies in this patient population.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at how a long-term lung disease called COPD and lung cancer often happen in the same person and how that affects care (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because people with COPD have a higher chance of getting lung cancer, but ways to stop cancer from starting are still very basic (Abstract, sentence 2). This work may help people who already have COPD, people at high risk for lung cancer, and the doctors who care for them (Abstract, sentence 1). The team read and summed up many past studies to explain how COPD and lung cancer are linked and how this changes care and outcomes (Abstract, sentence 6). They also looked at how well cancer checks, like lung scans, work in people with COPD (Abstract, sentence 3). They found that cancer checks can help people with COPD, but many people with COPD are never told they have it, so they may miss these checks (Abstract, sentence 3). They also found that lung cancer in people with COPD can look and act in a different way than in people without COPD (Abstract, sentence 4). Treating lung cancer is harder when COPD is present, with more problems after surgery and lower survival (Abstract, sentence 5). The authors suggest ways to better prevent cancer in people with COPD and to improve care for those who have both diseases (Abstract, sentence 6).

We need this study because many people have both COPD and lung cancer, and this makes treatment hard and can lower how long they live (Abstract, para. 1). If you have COPD, you also have a higher chance of getting lung cancer, even if you do not smoke now (Methods, para. 1). The writers of this paper did not test a new drug. They read and summed up many past studies on COPD, lung cancer risk, lung scans, surgery, and other treatments (Body, para. 2). They found that people with COPD are at higher risk for lung cancer, and that quitting smoking can cut lung cancer risk by about half over time (Methods, para. 1). Low‑dose chest scans can find lung cancer early in people with COPD and may help them live longer, but many people with COPD are never told they have it (Body, para. 5)(Body, para. 6). Surgery for lung cancer is more risky when you have COPD, but lung rehab, good lung drugs, and careful care can lower problems after surgery (Body, para. 12)(Body, para. 16). These findings may guide doctors to screen people with COPD sooner, support quitting smoking, and plan safer treatment for lung cancer in this group (Body, para. 23).

Title: Quantitative proteomics in lung cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death worldwide, less than 7% of patients survive 10 years following diagnosis across all stages of lung cancer. Late stage of diagnosis and lack of effective and personalized medicine reflect the need for a better understanding of the mechanisms that underlie lung cancer progression. Quantitative proteomics provides the relative different protein abundance in normal and cancer patients which offers the information for molecular interactions, signaling pathways, and biomarker identification. Here we introduce both theoretical and practical applications in the use of quantitative proteomics approaches, with principles of current technologies and methodologies including gel-based, label free, stable isotope labeling as well as targeted proteomics. Predictive markers of drug resistance, candidate biomarkers for diagnosis, and prognostic markers in lung cancer have also been discovered and analyzed by quantitative proteomic analysis. Moreover, construction of protein networks enables to provide an opportunity to interpret disease pathway and improve our understanding in cancer therapeutic strategies, allowing the discovery of molecular markers and new therapeutic targets for lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This study looks at lung cancer, which is the top cause of cancer death in the world, and only about 7 out of 100 people are still alive 10 years after they learn they have it (Abstract, sentence 1). We need better ways to find lung cancer early and to pick the right drug for each person, but we do not yet know enough about how this cancer grows and spreads (Abstract, sentence 2). The team used a lab method that can measure many proteins, which are tiny parts in your cells that do most of the work (Abstract, sentence 3). They compared proteins in normal lung cells and in lung cancer cells to see which ones change (Abstract, sentence 3). They also explain how this method works in real labs, using several types of tools to measure these proteins (Abstract, sentence 4). From this work, they found protein “markers” that may help tell who will not respond well to some drugs, who has lung cancer, and who may do better or worse over time (Abstract, sentence 5). They also built maps of how proteins link and talk to each other, to better see which paths in the cell drive lung cancer and may be good drug targets (Abstract, sentence 6). In the future, these protein markers may help doctors choose tests and drugs that fit each lung cancer patient more closely (Abstract, sentence 5).
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This research looks at lung cancer, which is the top cause of cancer death in the world, and asks how we can find it earlier and treat it in a more personal way (Abstract, para. 1). We need this work because most people with lung cancer do not live 10 years after they find out they are sick, and current care is often not enough, especially for the most common type called non‑small cell lung cancer (Introduction, para. 1). The team used a lab method called “quantitative proteomics,” which is a way to measure many proteins in blood, body fluid, or tissue and compare people with lung cancer to people without it (Introduction, para. 2). They reviewed four main lab approaches and how these can spot protein “markers” that signal cancer (Body, para. 1). They found many protein markers that may help with early lung cancer tests, tell who has a worse outlook, and show who may not respond well to some drugs (Body, para. 7). For example, some protein patterns in lung fluid and blood can help tell lung cancer from other lung disease and may pick up cancer at an early stage (Body, para. 10). These findings may one day help doctors choose the right drug for you and use simple lab tests to find lung cancer sooner, but they still need more testing in large patient groups (Body, para. 8).

Title: The Roles of MicroRNA in Lung Cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the most devastating malignancy in the world. Beyond genetic research, epigenomic studies-especially investigations of microRNAs-have grown rapidly in quantity and quality in the past decade. This has enriched our understanding about basic cancer biology and lit up the opportunities for potential therapeutic development. In this review, we summarize the involvement of microRNAs in lung cancer carcinogenesis and behavior, by illustrating the relationship to each cancer hallmark capability, and in addition, we briefly describe the clinical applications of microRNAs in lung cancer diagnosis and prognosis. Finally, we discuss the potential therapeutic use of microRNAs in lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at lung cancer, which is one of the deadliest types of cancer in the world (Abstract, sentence 1). The study may help people who have lung cancer now or who may get it in the future (Abstract, sentence 1). The writers do not test new drugs in people. Instead, they read and sum up many past lab and clinic studies about tiny gene control parts called microRNAs and how these link to lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). They look at how these tiny parts may help cancer cells grow, spread, and stay alive (Abstract, sentence 4). They find that work on microRNAs has grown fast in the last ten years and has helped us learn more about how cancer starts and acts (Abstract, sentence 2). They also show how microRNAs may help doctors tell who has lung cancer, how bad it is, and what may happen over time (Abstract, sentence 4). This may guide care choices, like when to watch more close or when to treat more hard (Abstract, sentence 4). The writers also talk about how microRNAs might one day be used as new treatments for lung cancer, but this is still early and needs more study (Abstract, sentence 3). In the future, these tiny gene control parts may help doctors better test for, predict, and treat lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 5).

Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death in the world, so we need better ways to find it, tell types apart, and choose treatment (Introduction, para. 1). This work may help people at high risk, people being tested for lung cancer, and people already in treatment (Body, para. 32). The writers read and summed up many lab and patient studies on how these small switches change cancer cell growth, spread, blood supply, and escape from the immune system (Body, para. 1). They also looked at how microRNAs in blood and tissue can act as lab tests and how they may change response to chemo, radiation, and drug pills that target cancer genes (Body, para. 32). They found that sets of microRNAs in blood can help tell who has lung cancer, with some tests showing about 75–87% accuracy in high‑risk groups (Body, para. 33). Other microRNAs link to how long people live and how well they respond to drugs or radiation (Body, para. 34). Early drug trials that add or block microRNAs in lung cancer show promise but also safety problems, so they are not ready for routine care yet (Body, para. 47). In the future, blood tests and treatments based on microRNAs may help guide lung cancer care, but more and larger studies are still needed (Conclusion, para. 1).

Title: Immunosurveillance and Immunoediting of Lung Cancer: Current Perspectives and Challenges.
Abstract: The immune system plays a dual role in tumor evolution-it can identify and control nascent tumor cells in a process called immunosurveillance and can promote tumor progression through immunosuppression via various mechanisms. Thus, bilateral host-protective and tumor-promoting actions of immunity are integrated as cancer immunoediting. In this decade, immune checkpoint inhibitors, specifically programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) pathway inhibitors, have changed the treatment paradigm of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). These agents are approved for the treatment of patients with NSCLC and demonstrate impressive clinical activity and durable responses in some patients. However, for many NSCLC patients, the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors is limited. To optimize the full utility of the immune system for eradicating cancer, a broader understanding of cancer immunosurveillance and immunoediting is essential. In this review, we discuss the fundamental knowledge of the phenomena and provide an overview of the next-generation immunotherapies in the pipeline.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at how your own defense system, called the immune system, can both fight and help lung cancer grow (Abstract, sentence 1). It focuses on a type of lung cancer called non‑small cell lung cancer and on new drugs that help the immune system see and attack cancer cells (Abstract, sentence 3). We need this study because some people with this lung cancer do very well on these drugs, but many others do not get much help from them (Abstract, sentence 4). This work may help people with advanced lung cancer and the doctors who treat them (Abstract, sentence 5). The team read and summed up many past studies to explain how the immune system first watches for and kills new cancer cells, but later can be turned off or even used by the cancer to grow (Abstract, sentence 1). They call this back‑and‑forth “immunoediting,” which means the immune system and cancer shape each other over time (Abstract, sentence 2). They also list new immune‑based drugs now being tested that may work better or help more people (Abstract, sentence 7). These findings matter because they can guide new drug plans that use the immune system in a smarter way to fight lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 6). In the future, this may lead to more treatment choices for people with this disease (Abstract, sentence 7).

Title: Lung Cancer Staging and Associated Genetic and Epigenetic Events.
Abstract: The first step in treating lung cancer is to establish the stage of the disease, which in turn determines the treatment options and prognosis of the patient. Many factors are involved in lung cancer staging, but all involve anatomical information. However, new approaches, mainly those based on the molecular biology of cancer, have recently changed the paradigm for lung cancer treatment and have not yet been incorporated into staging. In a group of patients of the same stage who receive the same treatment, some may experience unexpected recurrence or metastasis, largely because current staging methods do not reflect the findings of molecular biological studies. In this review, we provide a brief summary of the latest research on lung cancer staging and the molecular events associated with carcinogenesis. We hope that this paper will serve as a bridge between clinicians and basic researchers and aid in our understanding of lung cancer.

Title: Insights Into Lung Cancer Immune-Based Biology, Prevention, and Treatment.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the number one cause of cancer-related deaths. The malignancy is characterized by dismal prognosis and poor clinical outcome mostly due to advanced-stage at diagnosis, thereby inflicting a heavy burden on public health worldwide. Recent breakthroughs in immunotherapy have greatly benefited a subset of lung cancer patients, and more importantly, they are undauntedly bringing forth a paradigm shift in the drugs approved for cancer treatment, by introducing "tumor-type agnostic therapies". Yet, and to fulfill immunotherapy's potential of personalized cancer treatment, demarcating the immune and genomic landscape of cancers at their earliest possible stages will be crucial to identify ideal targets for early treatment and to predict how a particular patient will fare with immunotherapy. Recent genomic surveys of premalignant lung cancer have shed light on early alterations in the evolution of lung cancer. More recently, the advent of immunogenomic technologies has provided prodigious opportunities to study the multidimensional landscape of lung tumors as well as their microenvironment at the molecular, genomic, and cellular resolution. In this review, we will summarize the current state of immune-based therapies for cancer, with a focus on lung malignancy, and highlight learning outcomes from clinical and preclinical studies investigating the naïve immune biology of lung cancer. The review also collates immunogenomic-based evidence from seminal reports which collectively warrant future investigations of premalignancy, the tumor-adjacent normal-appearing lung tissue, pulmonary inflammatory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, as well as systemic microbiome imbalance. Such future directions enable novel insights into the evolution of lung cancers and, thus, can provide a low-hanging fruit of targets for early immune-based treatment of this fatal malignancy.

Lung cancer causes more deaths than any other cancer, and many people find out they have it only when it is very late (Abstract, sentence 1). Because of this late stage, many people do not do well, and this is a big health problem around the world (Abstract, sentence 2). The writers of this paper read and summed up many past lab and patient studies on immune based drugs for lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 7). Some new immune drugs already help a group of lung cancer patients and are changing which drugs doctors can use (Abstract, sentence 3). The paper also looks at early lung changes, even before full cancer forms, to see which gene changes and immune cells show up first (Abstract, sentence 5). New lab tools now let us study lung tumors and nearby lung tissue in great detail (Abstract, sentence 6). The writers say that if we map these early changes, we may find better targets for early care and may better guess who will gain from immune drugs (Abstract, sentence 4). In the future, this may lead to earlier and more personal lung cancer care and new ways to treat high risk lung tissue before it turns into full cancer (Abstract, sentence 8)(Abstract, sentence 9).

Title: New insights into small-cell lung cancer development and therapy.
Abstract: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) accounts for approximately 15% of lung cancer cases; however, it is characterized by easy relapse and low survival rate, leading to one of the most intractable diseases in clinical practice. Despite decades of basic and clinical research, little progress has been made in the management of SCLC. The current standard first-line regimens of SCLC still remain to be cisplatin or carboplatin combined with etoposide, and the adverse events of chemotherapy are by no means negligible. Besides, the immunotherapy on SCLC is still in an early stage and novel studies are urgently needed. In this review, we describe SCLC development and current therapy, aiming at providing useful advices on basic research and clinical strategy.
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at a fast‑growing lung cancer called small‑cell lung cancer, or SCLC (Abstract, sentence 1). It makes up about 15 out of 100 lung cancer cases and often comes back after treatment, so many people do not live long with it (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because, even after many years of work, doctors have not made much progress in how they treat this type of lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). This may help people who have SCLC now or may get it in the future (Abstract, sentence 1). The writers of this paper read and summed up many past studies on how SCLC starts and how doctors treat it now (Abstract, sentence 5). They looked at the main drug care, which still uses two drugs called cisplatin or carboplatin with another drug named etoposide (Abstract, sentence 3). These drugs can cause strong side effects that are hard for many people (Abstract, sentence 3). They also found that new “immune” drugs, which help your own body fight the cancer, are still very early in use for SCLC (Abstract, sentence 4). The paper ends by giving ideas to guide lab work and care plans for this disease (Abstract, sentence 5). In the future, this may help doctors plan kinder and better care for people with SCLC (Abstract, sentence 5).

Instead, they read and summed up many past studies on how SCLC starts, how it grows, and how doctors treat it now (Abstract, para. 1)(Conclusion, para. 1). Title: Gender-specific aspects of epidemiology, molecular genetics and outcome: lung cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide in women and men. In incidence, lung cancer ranks second, surpassed by breast cancer in women and prostate cancer in men. However, the historical differences in mortality and incidence rate between both sexes have changed in the last years. In the last decades, we have also witnessed an increased number of lung cancer in female never-smokers. These disparities have grown our interest in studying the impact of the gender and sex in the presentation of lung cancer. The aetiology is yet to be fully elucidated, but the data are clear so far: there is a growing divide between lung cancer presentation in women and men that will change our management and study of lung cancer. This article aims to review the sex and gender differences in lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at how lung cancer is different in women and men (Abstract, sentence 7). Lung cancer is the top cause of death from cancer for both women and men, so this is a big health problem (Abstract, sentence 1). It is also the second most common cancer, after breast cancer in women and prostate cancer in men (Abstract, sentence 2). In recent years, the gap in how often women and men get and die from lung cancer has changed (Abstract, sentence 3). We now see more lung cancer in women who have never smoked, which raises new questions (Abstract, sentence 4). Because of these changes, the team wanted to learn how sex and gender may shape who gets lung cancer and how it shows up (Abstract, sentence 5). The writers did a review, which means they read and summed up many past studies on lung cancer in women and men (Abstract, sentence 7). They found clear signs that lung cancer can look and act different in women than in men (Abstract, sentence 6). These results matter because they may change how we test, treat, and study lung cancer in the future (Abstract, sentence 6). This could help doctors give more “fit for you” care to both women and men with lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 6).

It may help people at risk for lung cancer, and those who plan tests and treatment (Introduction, para. 8). The team read many past studies and reports from large health groups to compare lung cancer rates, risks, and outcomes by sex and gender (Introduction, para. 9). They also looked at work risks, home air, smoking, and secondhand smoke (Introduction, para. 3). They found more women who never smoked now get lung cancer than men who never smoked, and in some areas over half of women with lung cancer never smoked (Introduction, para. 7). Women may be more at risk from the same amount of smoke, and they often find it harder to quit (Body, para. 2). These results suggest scan rules and care plans may need to fit women and men differently in the future (Conclusion, para. 2).

Title: Update 2020: Management of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
Abstract: The past decade has seen a revolution of new advances in the management of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with remarkable progresses in screening, diagnosis, and treatment. The advances in systemic treatment have been driven primarily by the development of molecularly targeted therapeutics, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and anti-angiogenic agents, all of which have transformed this field with significantly improved patient outcomes. This review will address updates in lung cancer screening, liquid biopsy, and immunotherapy in the front-line setting. We discuss recent advances and highlight the plethora of new approvals of molecular-targeted therapy for subgroups of NSCLC patients with sensitizing EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, BRAF V600E, MET, and NTRK alterations.
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at new ways to find and treat a common type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer, or NSCLC (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because many people still die from this cancer, and better tests and drugs can help them live longer and feel better (Abstract, sentence 1). The writers of the paper read and summed up many other studies on lung scans to find cancer early, blood tests to look for cancer signs, and new drug types that help the body fight cancer (Abstract, sentence 3). They also looked at drugs that block blood flow to tumors and drugs that target very exact gene changes in the cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). They found that these new drugs and tests have greatly raised how long many people with this lung cancer can live (Abstract, sentence 2). Some drugs work only in people whose tumors have certain gene changes, such as EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, BRAF V600E, MET, or NTRK (Abstract, sentence 4). These results matter because they show that care for this lung cancer is changing fast and can now be more “made to fit” for each person (Abstract, sentence 2). In the future, more people may get a blood test and gene test on their tumor to help pick the best drug for them (Abstract, sentence 3).

You may benefit from this if you smoke now, smoked in the past, or have lung cancer, or care for someone who does. The team reviewed large past studies on lung scan tests, blood tests, and new cancer drugs. They looked at how low‑dose chest scans, called CT scans, can find cancer early in people at high risk. They also looked at “liquid biopsy,” which is a blood test that can find gene changes in the cancer and help guide drug choice when a tissue sample is hard to get. They found that CT scans cut the chance of death from lung cancer by about 20–33% in people at high risk. New targeted drugs and immune drugs also help people with advanced NSCLC live longer than with older chemo alone. These results support wider use of lung scan checks in high‑risk people and more testing of tumors to match each person with the best drug plan.

Title: Progress on pivotal role and application of exosome in lung cancer carcinogenesis, diagnosis, therapy and prognosis.
Abstract: Lung cancer is often diagnosed at an advanced stage and has a poor prognosis. Conventional treatments are not effective for metastatic lung cancer therapy. Although some of molecular targets have been identified with favorable response, those targets cannot be exploited due to the lack of suitable drug carriers. Lung cancer cell-derived exosomes (LCCDEs) receive recent interest in its role in carcinogenesis, diagnosis, therapy, and prognosis of lung cancer due to its biological functions and natural ability to carry donor cell biomolecules. LCCDEs can promote cell proliferation and metastasis, affect angiogenesis, modulate antitumor immune responses during lung cancer carcinogenesis, regulate drug resistance in lung cancer therapy, and be now considered an important component in liquid biopsy assessments for detecting lung cancer. Therapeutic deliverable exosomes are emerging as promising drug delivery agents specifically to tumor high precision medicine because of their natural intercellular communication role, excellent biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, low toxicity, long blood circulation ability, biodegradable characteristics, and their ability to cross various biological barriers. Several studies are currently underway to develop novel diagnostic and prognostic modalities using LCCDEs, and to develop methods of exploiting exosomes for use as efficient drug delivery vehicles. Current status of lung cancer and extensive applicability of LCCDEs are illustrated in this review. The promising data and technologies indicate that the approach on LCCDEs implies the potential application of LCCDEs to clinical management of lung cancer patients.
Abstract_Summary: This study looks at a tiny bubble from lung cancer cells, called an exosome, and how we may use it to find and treat lung cancer in the future (Abstract, sentence 4). We need this work because lung cancer is often found late and is hard to cure (Abstract, sentence 1). Usual drugs do not work well once the cancer has spread to other parts of the body (Abstract, sentence 2). Some drug targets look hopeful, but we do not yet have good ways to carry these drugs to the tumor (Abstract, sentence 3). The writers of this paper read and summed up many past lab and clinic studies on lung cancer cell exosomes (Abstract, sentence 8). They looked at how these tiny bubbles help cancer grow, spread, and fight off drugs, and how they might be used in blood tests (Abstract, sentence 5). They found that these exosomes can help cancer cells grow and move, change blood flow to tumors, and change how the body’s defense cells act (Abstract, sentence 5). They also found that exosomes may work as safe, natural drug bags that can move through the blood and reach tumors (Abstract, sentence 6). New studies now test exosomes as tools for blood tests and as drug carriers for lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 7). Early data suggest they may one day help doctors better test and treat people with lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 9).

Title: Role of lung and gut microbiota on lung cancer pathogenesis.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide (Ferlay et al., Int J Cancer 136:E359-386, 2015). In addition, lung cancer is associated with the highest mortality among all cancer types (Wu et al., Exp Ther Med 16:3004-3010, 2018). Previous studies report that microbiota play an important role in lung cancer. Notably, changes in lung and gut microbiota, are associated with progression of lung cancer. Several studies report that lung and gut microbiome promote lung cancer initiation and development by modulating metabolic pathways, inhibiting the function of immune cells, and producing pro-inflammatory factors. In addition, some factors such as microbiota dysbiosis, affect production of bacteriotoxins, genotoxicity and virulence effect, therefore, they play a key role in cancer progression. These findings imply that lung and gut microbiome are potential markers and targets for lung cancer. However, the role of microbiota in development and progression of lung cancer has not been fully explored. PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to systemically review recent research findings on relationship of lung and gut microbiota with lung cancer. In addition, we explored gut-lung axis and potential mechanisms of lung and gut microbiota in modulating lung cancer progression. CONCLUSION: Pulmonary and intestinal flora influence the occurrence, development, treatment and prognosis of lung cancer, and will provide novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This study looks at tiny germs that live in your lungs and gut, and how they link to lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 5). Lung cancer causes more deaths than any other cancer, so we need better ways to find, treat, and prevent it (Abstract, sentence 1). This work may help people who have lung cancer now, or who are at high risk for it in the future (Abstract, sentence 3). The team did not test new drugs or follow one group of patients (Abstract, sentence 11). Instead, they read and summed up many recent studies on lung and gut germs and lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 11). They also looked at how germs in the gut and lungs may “talk” to each other and to the lungs, which they call the gut–lung link (Abstract, sentence 12). They found that changes in lung and gut germs are tied to how lung cancer starts and grows (Abstract, sentence 6). These germs may help cancer grow by changing how the body makes and uses energy, by slowing the body’s defense cells, and by making strong “alarm” signals that cause long-term swelling (Abstract, sentence 7). The writers say that lung and gut germs may be used in the future as signs to spot lung cancer or as targets for new care (Abstract, sentence 9). This could one day guide new tests and treatments for lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 13).

Title: Host-Microbiome Interaction in Lung Cancer.
Abstract: Commensal microbiota has emerged as an essential biomarker and regulator of both tumorigenesis and response to cancer therapy. However, our current knowledge about microbiota in cancer has been largely limited to intestinal microbiota. As a mucosal organ harboring one of the largest surface areas in the body, the lung is exposed to a variety of microbes through inhalation and micro-aspiration, and is colonized by a diverse bacterial community in both physiological and pathological conditions. Importantly, increasing evidence has linked the lung microbiome to cancer development. Studies in lung cancer patients and mouse models have revealed tumor-associated dysregulation of the local microbiome in the lung, which in turn impacts cancer progression by shaping the tumor microenvironment and modulating the activity of tumor-infiltrating immune cells. These findings not only provide novel mechanistic insight into the biology of lung cancer but also shed light on new therapeutic targets and strategies for lung cancer prevention and treatment. The goal of this review is to discuss the key findings, remaining questions, and future directions in this new and exciting field.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at tiny germs, called microbes, that live in and on your body, and how they link to lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 1). We already know that germs in the gut can affect cancer and how well cancer drugs work, but we know much less about germs in the lung (Abstract, sentence 1). This work may help people who have lung cancer now or who are at risk for it in the future (Abstract, sentence 2). Your lungs have a very large wet surface that touches the air you breathe, so many kinds of germs can live there, even when you feel well (Abstract, sentence 3). In this study, the writers read and summed up many past lab and patient studies on lung germs and lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 7). They found that changes in the normal lung germs are linked to lung cancer growth (Abstract, sentence 4). In both people and mice, lung tumors often show a “mixed up” germ group that can change the area around the tumor and the work of immune cells that enter the tumor (Abstract, sentence 5). These results help us better grasp how lung cancer starts and grows and point to new ways to prevent or treat it by also targeting lung germs (Abstract, sentence 6). In the future, doctors may test or adjust lung germs to help guide lung cancer care (Abstract, sentence 6).

It may help people who have lung cancer now or who are at high risk, such as people who smoke (Introduction, para. 2). The writers read and pulled together many past studies that used new lab tools to count and name germs in lung tissue, lung fluid, and gut samples from people and mice (Body, para. 1). They then compared people with lung cancer to people without cancer (Body, para. 4). They found that lungs are not empty; they hold many kinds of germs, and this mix changes in lung cancer (Body, para. 1). In cancer, there are often more total germs but fewer types, and more germs that usually live in the mouth (Body, para. 5). The authors say that, in the future, certain lung germs might help doctors spot lung cancer earlier or guide new treatments that target these germs (Body, para. 13)(Body, para. 16).

Title: Current and Future Development in Lung Cancer Diagnosis.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America and other developed countries. One of the reasons lung cancer is at the top of the list is that it is often not diagnosed until the cancer is at an advanced stage. Thus, the earliest diagnosis of lung cancer is crucial, especially in screening high-risk populations, such as smokers, exposure to fumes, oil fields, toxic occupational places, etc. Based on the current knowledge, it looks that there is an urgent need to identify novel biomarkers. The current diagnosis of lung cancer includes different types of imaging complemented with pathological assessment of biopsies, but these techniques can still not detect early lung cancer developments. In this review, we described the advantages and disadvantages of current methods used in diagnosing lung cancer, and we provide an analysis of the potential use of body fluids as carriers of biomarkers as predictors of cancer development and progression.
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at how we can find lung cancer earlier and in a more gentle way for you as a patient (Abstract, sentence 6). Lung cancer causes more deaths than any other cancer in rich countries (Abstract, sentence 1). One big reason is that we often do not find it until it is very late and hard to treat (Abstract, sentence 2). People who smoke or work around fumes or toxic places have a higher risk and need better early tests (Abstract, sentence 3). Today, doctors use scans and a small piece of lung tissue to find lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 5). These tests can be painful or scary and still may miss very early cancer (Abstract, sentence 5). The writers of this paper looked at how well these tests work and where they fall short (Abstract, sentence 6). They also looked at signs of cancer that may float in blood, spit, or other body fluids (Abstract, sentence 6). These signs are called “markers” and may help tell if cancer is there or growing (Abstract, sentence 4). If these body fluid markers prove to work well, they may one day help doctors test people at high risk sooner and with less pain (Abstract, sentence 3).

Lung cancer causes more deaths than any other cancer, in part because most people are not told they have it until it is in a late stage (Introduction, para. 1). This work may help people at high risk, such as long‑time smokers and people who breathe in toxic fumes at work (Introduction, para. 2). The team reviews current tests like chest scans and scopes into the lung, and explains that these can miss small, early tumors and can be costly or uncomfortable (Introduction, para. 3). They then look at many new lab tests that use body fluids such as blood, spit, and urine to search for “biomarkers,” which are signs of cancer in the body (Introduction, para. 4). New blood tests, called liquid biopsies, may also help guide treatment and track how well it works, but they still need better accuracy (Body, para. 46). The authors say future lung cancer tests will likely be simple fluid tests that cause less discomfort and cost, and that can be done often to help find cancer sooner (Conclusion, para. 3).

Title: Tumor-associated exosomes promote lung cancer metastasis through multiple mechanisms.
Abstract: As an important medium of intercellular communication, exosomes play an important role in information transmission between tumor cells and their microenvironment. Tumor metastasis is a serious influencing factor for poor treatment effect and shortened survival. Lung cancer is a major malignant tumor that seriously threatens human health. The study of the underlying mechanisms of exosomes in tumor genesis and development may provide new ideas for early and effective diagnosis and treatment of lung cancer metastasis. Many studies have shown that tumor-derived exosomes promote lung cancer development through a number of processes. By promoting epithelial-mesenchymal transition of tumor cells, they induce angiogenesis, establishment of the pretransfer microenvironment, and immune escape. This understanding enables researchers to better understand the mechanism of lung cancer metastasis and explore new treatments for clinical application. In this article, we systematically review current research progress of tumor-derived exosomes in metastasis of lung cancer. Although positive progress has been made toward understanding the mechanism of exosomes in lung cancer metastasis, systematic basic research and clinical translational research remains lacking and are needed to translate our scientific understanding toward applications in the clinical diagnosis and treatment of lung cancer metastasis in the near future.

Lung cancer is a major cause of poor health and death, so we need better ways to find and treat it (Abstract, sentence 3). When lung cancer spreads, or “metastasis,” it often makes treatment work less well and can shorten life (Abstract, sentence 2). The writers of this paper did not test new drugs in people (Abstract, sentence 8). Instead, they read and summed up many past lab and animal studies on exosomes in lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 8). They looked at how these tiny bubbles move signals between cancer cells and nearby cells (Abstract, sentence 1). They found that exosomes from tumors can help lung cancer grow and spread in many ways (Abstract, sentence 5). These bubbles can help cancer cells change shape, grow new blood tubes, and hide from the body’s defense system (Abstract, sentence 6). This work may help us find new lab tests and new drug targets for lung cancer that has spread (Abstract, sentence 4). But the writers say we still need more basic and clinic research before this can help you or other patients in real life (Abstract, sentence 9).

Title: Gender Differences and Immunotherapy Outcome in Advanced Lung Cancer.
Abstract: In developed countries, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in both sexes. Although cigarette smoking represents the principal risk factor for lung cancer in females, the higher proportion of this neoplasm among non-smoking women as compared with non-smoking men implies distinctive biological aspects between the two sexes. Gender differences depend not only on genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors but also on the immune system, and all these aspects are closely interconnected. In the last few years, it has been confirmed that the immune system plays a fundamental role in cancer evolution and response to oncological treatments, specifically immunotherapy, with documented distinctions between men and women. Consequently, in order to correctly assess cancer responses and disease control, considering only age and reproductive status, the results of studies conducted in female patients would probably not categorically apply to male patients and vice versa. The aim of this article is to review recent data about gender disparities in both healthy subjects' immune system and lung cancer patients; furthermore, studies concerning gender differences in response to lung cancer immunotherapy are examined.

We need this study because lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death in rich countries for both men and women (Abstract, sentence 1). It may help people with lung cancer and the doctors who choose their care (Abstract, sentence 6). Smoking is still the main risk for lung cancer in women, but more women who never smoke get this cancer than men who never smoke (Abstract, sentence 2). This hints that the cancer may act in a different way in women (Abstract, sentence 2). The team did not test a new drug (Abstract, sentence 6). They read and summed up many past studies on how men’s and women’s immune systems differ, both in health and in lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 3)(Abstract, sentence 6). They also looked at past work on how men and women respond to new cancer drugs that help the immune system fight tumors (Abstract, sentence 4)(Abstract, sentence 6). They found that genes, hormones, the world around us, and the immune system all link to sex and can change how lung cancer grows and how well treatment works (Abstract, sentence 3)(Abstract, sentence 4). These results mean we may need to test and judge lung cancer drugs in men and women on their own, not as one group (Abstract, sentence 5).

Title: The Immunotherapy for Colorectal Cancer, Lung Cancer and Pancreatic Cancer.
Abstract: Immunotherapy is a novel anti-cancer method which employs a different mechanism to conventional treatment. It has become a significant strategy because it provides a better or an alternative option for cancer patients. Recently, immunotherapy has been increasingly approved for the treatment of cancer; however, it has various limitations; for instance, it is only suitable for specific patients, the response rate is still low in most cases, etc. Colorectal cancer, lung cancer and pancreatic cancer are known as three major death-causing cancers in most countries. In this review, we discuss immunotherapeutic treatment for these three cancers, and consider the option, prospects and limitations of immunotherapy. The development of immunotherapy should focus on the discovery of biomarkers to screen suitable patients, new targets on tumors, neoadjuvant immunotherapy and the combination of immunotherapy with conventional therapeutic methods. We can expect that immunotherapy potentially will develop as one of the best therapies for patients with advanced cancer or poor responses to traditional methods.
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at a type of cancer care called immunotherapy, which helps your own body fight cancer in a new way (Abstract, sentence 1). The work focuses on three common and deadly cancers: colon and rectal cancer, lung cancer, and pancreatic cancer (Abstract, sentence 4). The study is needed because many people with these cancers do not do well with standard care like surgery, drugs, or radiation (Abstract, sentence 2). Immunotherapy can give some people a better or extra choice when other care does not work well (Abstract, sentence 2). The writers of the paper read and summed up many past studies on how immunotherapy is used in these three cancers (Abstract, sentence 5). They also looked at how well it works, who it helps, and where it falls short (Abstract, sentence 3). They found that more and more cancer care teams now use immunotherapy, but it does not help every person (Abstract, sentence 3). It works best in some groups, and many people still do not get a strong response (Abstract, sentence 3). The team says we need better lab tests to pick the right people, new targets on tumor cells, and smart ways to mix immunotherapy with older care (Abstract, sentence 6). If these steps work, immunotherapy may become one of the best choices for people with late-stage cancer or poor response to usual care (Abstract, sentence 7).

Title: [Lung Cancer Stem-like Cells and Drug Resistance].
Abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related death world-wide. Therapy resistance and relapse are considered major reasons contributing to the poor survival rates of lung cancer. Accumulated evidences have demonstrated that a small subpopulation of stem-like cells existed within lung cancer tissues and cell lines, possessing the abilities of self-renewal, multipotent differentiation and unlimited proliferation. These lung cancer stem-like cells (LCSCs) can generate tumors with high effeciency in vivo, survive cytotoxic therapies, and eventually lead to therapy resistance and recurrence. In this review, we would like to present recent knowledges on LCSCs, including the origins where they come from, the molecular features to identify them, and key mechanisms for them to survive and develop resistance, in order to provide a better view for targeting them in future clinic. .
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at a special small group of cells inside lung tumors called lung cancer stem‑like cells, or LCSCs (Abstract, sentence 3). We need this study because lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death in the world, and many people die when the cancer comes back after treatment (Abstract, sentence 1). Therapy often stops working over time, and this “therapy resistance” is a big reason why people with lung cancer do not live as long as we hope (Abstract, sentence 2). In this work, the writers did not test new drugs in people (Abstract, sentence 5). They read and summed up many past lab and animal studies to explain where these stem‑like cells come from, how to spot them, and how they stay alive during treatment (Abstract, sentence 5). They found that LCSCs can make many new tumor cells, can keep growing without limit, and can form new tumors very easily in animals (Abstract, sentence 3). These cells can also live through strong cancer drugs and can help the cancer come back later (Abstract, sentence 4). These findings matter because if we can find and block these stem‑like cells, we may stop tumors from coming back after treatment in the future (Abstract, sentence 5).

Title: MicroRNA in lung cancer-a novel potential way for early diagnosis and therapy.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related deaths in the world. One of the reasons of poor prognosis and high mortality of lung cancer patients is the diagnosis of the disease in its advanced stage. Despite innovative diagnostic methods and multiple completed and ongoing clinical trials aiming at therapy improvement, no significant increase in patients' long-term survival has been noted over last decades. Patients would certainly benefit from early detection of lung cancer. Therefore, it is crucial to find new biomarkers that can help predict outcomes and tumor responses in order to maximize therapy effectiveness and avoid over- or under-treating patients with lung cancer. Nowadays, scientists' attention is mainly dedicated to so-called liquid biopsy, which is fully non-invasive and easily available method based on simple blood draw. Among common liquid biopsy elements, circulating tumor nucleic acids are worth mentioning. Epigenetic biomarkers, particularly miRNA expression, have several distinct features that make them promising prognostic markers. In this review, we described miRNA's involvement in tumorigenesis and present it as a predictor of cancer development and progression, potential indicator of treatment efficacy, and most importantly promising therapeutic target.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at lung cancer, which is the top cause of cancer death in the world (Abstract, sentence 1). Many people learn they have lung cancer only when it is at a late stage, which makes it hard to treat and leads to more deaths (Abstract, sentence 2). Even with new tests and many drug studies, people with lung cancer have not seen big gains in long-term survival over many years (Abstract, sentence 3). So we need better ways to find lung cancer early and to match each person with the right treatment (Abstract, sentence 4). The writers of this paper review work on “liquid biopsy,” which is a test that uses a simple blood draw instead of a tissue sample from the lung (Abstract, sentence 6). In the blood, they look at tiny bits from the tumor, called tumor nucleic acids (Abstract, sentence 7). They focus on small gene control parts called miRNA, which can act as signs, or “markers,” of how a tumor starts, grows, and responds to treatment (Abstract, sentence 8). They report that miRNA patterns may help tell how the cancer will act, how well treatment may work, and may even be used as a new kind of treatment target in the future (Abstract, sentence 9). If later studies confirm this, blood tests for miRNA could one day help doctors choose better care for people with lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 5).

You and other patients could do better if we find the cancer early and choose the right treatment for each person (Introduction, para. 4). In this study, teams looked at many reports on microRNAs in lung cancer. They checked how these small markers change in cancer cells and in blood, and how those changes link to cancer type, spread, and patient survival (Body, para. 4). They also reviewed tests that measure microRNAs from a simple blood draw, called a “liquid biopsy” (Body, para. 39). They found that certain microRNAs are often higher or lower in lung cancer and can help tell cancer types apart and predict how long people live (Body, para. 6). These results matter because blood microRNA tests may one day help doctors spot lung cancer sooner and track how well treatment works, but more large, careful studies are still needed before they become routine in care (Conclusion, para. 1)(Conclusion, para. 2).

Title: Vistas in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) Treatment: of Kinome and Signaling Networks.
Abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the prevailing lung cancer type, accounting for ~85% of all lung cancer cases. Despite their initial promise, current chemotherapeutic protocols are reaching their limits. This necessitates the prompt discovery of new molecular drivers and the development of novel regimens for advanced NSCLC. Herein, we pose that there is a need to systematically profile the human kinome activity of NSCLC. Using available state-of-the-art technologies, a wide gamut of kinase activities can be simultaneously mapped and quantified specifically in the primary or metastatic cancer states, with oncogenic kinase functions being likely linked to mutation signatures and malignant features of NSCLC. New chemical compound libraries can then be screened for kinase inhibitory properties in preclinical model systems, with presumptive induction of programmed cell-death subroutines and signaling-disintegration routes serving as major outputs of novel inhibitor tumor-suppressor potentials.

They can then test many new lab-made drug mixes to see which ones turn off these kinase switches and make cancer cells die in lab models (Abstract, sentence 6). If this work goes well, it may guide new drug tests for people with this type of lung cancer in the future (Abstract, sentence 3).

Title: MiRNA-Based Therapies for Lung Cancer: Opportunities and Challenges?
Abstract: Lung cancer is a commonly diagnosed cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths, posing a serious health risk. Despite new advances in immune checkpoint and targeted therapies in recent years, the prognosis for lung cancer patients, especially those in advanced stages, remains poor. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have been shown to modulate tumor development at multiple levels, and as such, miRNA mimics and molecules aimed at regulating miRNAs have shown promise in preclinical development. More importantly, miRNA-based therapies can also complement conventional chemoradiotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapies to reverse drug resistance and increase the sensitivity of lung cancer cells. Furthermore, small interfering RNA (siRNA) and miRNA-based therapies have entered clinical trials and have shown favorable development prospects. Therefore, in this paper, we review recent advances in miRNA-based therapies in lung cancer treatment as well as adjuvant therapy and present the current state of clinical lung cancer treatment. We also discuss the challenges facing miRNA-based therapies in the clinical application of lung cancer treatment to provide new ideas for the development of novel lung cancer therapies.

Even with new drugs that help the body’s own defense system and drugs that target cancer cells, many people with lung cancer, most of all in late stages, still do not do well (Abstract, sentence 2). The writers of this paper did not test a new drug in people (Abstract, sentence 6). They read and summed up many past lab and clinic studies on microRNA care for lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 6). They also looked at how these tools might work with chemo, radiation, and newer drugs to help those drugs work better and fight drug “resist,” when cancer stops responding to a drug (Abstract, sentence 4). They found that some microRNA and similar tools have already gone into early human tests and look hopeful so far (Abstract, sentence 5). The paper also talks about hard parts, like how to get these tools safely into lung cancer cells in real life care (Abstract, sentence 7). If future studies solve these hard parts, microRNA care may one day be used along with standard lung cancer care to help some patients live longer and feel better (Abstract, sentence 4).

Title: miRNA as biomarker in lung cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer has a high prevalence and mortality due to its late diagnosis and limited treatment, so it is essential to find biomarkers that allow a faster diagnosis and improve the survival of these patients. In this sense, biomarkers based on miRNAs have supposed a considerable advance. miRNAs, which are small RNA sequences, can regulate gene expression, so they play an essential role not only as a diagnostic biomarker but also as a therapeutic and prognostic one. Also, miRNA biomarkers can be obtained from liquid biopsies, which are less intrusive than lung biopsies, and have better accessibility, safety and repeatability, which allows using those biomarkers both for diagnosis and monitoring of patients. In this review, we highlight the importance of miRNAs and collect the existing evidence of their relationship with lung cancer.

Lung cancer is often found late, and many people die from it, so we need better ways to test and treat it (Abstract, sentence 1). The team studied tiny parts in cells called “miRNAs,” which can change how genes work in the body (Abstract, sentence 3). These miRNAs can act as signs that cancer is there, and they may also help guide treatment and tell how the illness may go over time (Abstract, sentence 3). We review many past studies to see how miRNAs link to lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 5). We also look at how these miRNA signs can be found in a simple blood draw, called a liquid biopsy, instead of a lung tissue sample (Abstract, sentence 4). A blood test is less painful, safer, and easier to repeat than a lung biopsy (Abstract, sentence 4). The review finds that miRNA markers are a big step forward for lung cancer tests (Abstract, sentence 2). In the future, these blood tests may help doctors find lung cancer earlier and watch how you respond to treatment (Abstract, sentence 4).

Title: COVID-19 and lung cancer.
Abstract: COVID-19 pandemic had affected health services around the world, also reducing the diagnosis of lung cancer. On the other hand, examination of surgical specimens in patients with lung cancer and SARS-CoV-2 gave the opportunity to evidence early histologic features related to this emerging pandemic. Different prioritization of health organizations during COVID-19 pandemic resulted in a significant decline of lung cancer screening (up to 56%), delayed diagnosis (up to 30-40%) and higher advanced stage, with some exceptions (i.e., Canada). Increased use of stereotactic radiation treatments in stage I-IIA have been noticed in better-organized health systems. Surgical specimens performed for lung cancer in patients with incipient SARS-CoV-2 permitted to appreciate early histologic findings of COVID-19 with hyperplastic pneumocytes with/without fibrin exudate, alveolar macrophages/myeloid cells, perivascular T-lymphocytic infiltrate and lack of hyaline membrane. While the COVID-19 pandemic has declined the rate of lung cancer diagnosis worldwide, some institutions have significantly limited detrimental effects. Histology related to early SARS-CoV-2 infection in surgical samples for lung cancer revealed specific histologic changes.

We need this study because during COVID-19, many health plans cut back on cancer checks, which led to fewer lung cancer tests and more late-stage cases (Abstract, sentence 3). This may affect you or someone you know who had care delayed (Abstract, sentence 6). The team looked at health records to see how often lung cancer was found and treated during the pandemic (Abstract, sentence 1). They also studied lung tissue removed during surgery from people who had early COVID-19 at the same time as lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). They found lung cancer checks dropped by up to 56%, and diagnosis was delayed by up to 30–40% in many places (Abstract, sentence 3). Some health systems stayed better organized and used more precise radiation instead of surgery for early lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 4). In lung tissue from people with early COVID-19, they saw clear, early changes in the lung cells and immune cells (Abstract, sentence 5). These results show that strong health systems can soften harm from a crisis and that lung tissue from cancer surgery can help us learn how a new virus harms the lung (Abstract, sentence 6). This may guide how doctors plan cancer care and lung checks in future outbreaks (Abstract, sentence 7).

Title: From osimertinib to preemptive combinations.
Abstract: Here, I suggest that while first-line osimertinib extends median progression-free survival (PFS) in EGFR-mutant lung cancer compared to first-generation TKIs, it reduces individual PFS in 15-20% of patients compared to first-generation TKIs. Since detecting a single resistant cell before treatment is usually impossible, osimertinib must be used in all patients as a first-line treatment, raising median PFS overall but harming some. The simplest remedy is a preemptive combination (PC) of osimertinib and gefitinib. A comprehensive PC (osimertinib, afatinib/gefitinib, and capmatinib) could dramatically increase PFS for 80% of patients compared to osimertinib alone, without harming anyone. This article also explores PCs for MET-driven lung cancer.

Title: Liquid biopsy techniques and lung cancer: diagnosis, monitoring and evaluation.
Abstract: Lung cancer stands as the most prevalent form of cancer globally, posing a significant threat to human well-being. Due to the lack of effective and accurate early diagnostic methods, many patients are diagnosed with advanced lung cancer. Although surgical resection is still a potential means of eradicating lung cancer, patients with advanced lung cancer usually miss the best chance for surgical treatment, and even after surgical resection patients may still experience tumor recurrence. Additionally, chemotherapy, the mainstay of treatment for patients with advanced lung cancer, has the potential to be chemo-resistant, resulting in poor clinical outcomes. The emergence of liquid biopsies has garnered considerable attention owing to their noninvasive nature and the ability for continuous sampling. Technological advancements have propelled circulating tumor cells (CTCs), circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), extracellular vesicles (EVs), tumor metabolites, tumor-educated platelets (TEPs), and tumor-associated antigens (TAA) to the forefront as key liquid biopsy biomarkers, demonstrating intriguing and encouraging results for early diagnosis and prognostic evaluation of lung cancer. This review provides an overview of molecular biomarkers and assays utilized in liquid biopsies for lung cancer, encompassing CTCs, ctDNA, non-coding RNA (ncRNA), EVs, tumor metabolites, TAAs and TEPs. Furthermore, we expound on the practical applications of liquid biopsies, including early diagnosis, treatment response monitoring, prognostic evaluation, and recurrence monitoring in the context of lung cancer.

Title: Emerging Targets in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer is responsible for a high burden of disease globally. Over the last two decades, the discovery of targetable oncogenic genomic alterations has revolutionized the treatment landscape for early-stage and advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). New molecular drivers continue to emerge as promising therapeutic targets, including KRAS non-G12C, RAF/MEK, HER3, Nectin-4, folate receptor alpha, ITGB6, and PRMT5. In this review, we summarize the emerging molecular targets with a potential clinical impact in advanced NSCLC, elaborating on their clinical characteristics and specific mechanisms and molecular pathways for which targeted treatments are currently available. Additionally, we present an aggregate of ongoing clinical trials investigating the available treatment options targeting such alterations, in addition to their current recruitment status and preliminary efficacy data. These advancements may guide further research endeavors and inform future treatment strategies to improve the management of and transform outcomes for patients with advanced NSCLC.

Lung cancer causes a lot of sickness and death around the world, so we need better and more exact care for people with this disease (Abstract, sentence 1). Over the last 20 years, we have found many gene changes in lung cancer cells that we can target with new drugs (Abstract, sentence 2). These “targeted” drugs aim at the cancer cells and can help in both early and late stages of NSCLC (Abstract, sentence 2). In this study, the team reviews new gene and protein targets, such as KRAS, RAF, HER3, Nectin-4, and others, that may be used for future drugs (Abstract, sentence 3). The writers looked at many past studies and lab tests to explain how these targets work in the body and how drugs might block them (Abstract, sentence 4). They also list current drug trials, how many people they are trying to enroll, and early signs of how well the drugs work (Abstract, sentence 5). These findings may help doctors plan new studies and build better treatment plans for people with advanced NSCLC in the future (Abstract, sentence 6). Over time, this may lead to more choices and better outcomes for patients with this lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 6).

Title: MicroRNAs in Lung Cancer Brain Metastasis.
Abstract: Brain metastasis is a significant clinical challenge for patients with advanced lung cancer, occurring in about 20-40% of cases. Brain metastasis causes severe neurological symptoms, leading to a poor prognosis and contributing significantly to lung cancer-related mortality. However, the underlying molecular mechanism behind brain metastasis remains largely unknown. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small, non-coding RNAs linked to several aspects of cancer progression, including metastasis. In the context of lung cancer, significant research has shown the involvement of miRNAs in regulating critical pathways related to metastatic spread to the brain. This review summarizes the scientific evidence regarding the regulatory roles of intra- and extracellular miRNAs, which specifically drive the spread of lung cancer cells to the brain. It also revises the known molecular mechanisms of brain metastasis, focusing on those from lung cancer as the primary tumor to better understand the complex mechanisms underlying this regulation. Understanding these complex regulatory mechanisms holds promise for developing novel diagnostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic strategies in brain metastasis.

Brain spread happens in about 20 to 40 out of 100 people with advanced lung cancer and is very hard to treat (Abstract, sentence 1). It can cause bad brain and nerve signs, shorten life, and is a major cause of death in lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). We need this study so we can better spot and treat brain spread in people with lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 3). It may help people who have lung cancer now or are at high risk for brain spread (Abstract, sentence 1). The team did not test new drugs but read and summed up many past lab and clinic studies (Abstract, sentence 6). They looked at how microRNAs inside and outside cells can push lung cancer cells to move and grow in the brain (Abstract, sentence 5). They also pulled together what is known about how brain spread starts and grows at the gene and cell level (Abstract, sentence 7). They found that certain microRNAs can drive or block brain spread in lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 6). This new map of how brain spread works may guide new lab tests to find risk early and new drug ideas to slow or stop spread to the brain (Abstract, sentence 8).

Title: Lung cancer and obesity: A contentious relationship (Review).
Abstract: The global obesity epidemic, attributed to sedentary lifestyles, unhealthy diets, genetics and environmental factors, has led to over 1.9 billion adults being classified as overweight and 650 million living with obesity. Despite advancements in early detection and treatment, lung cancer prognosis remains poor due to late diagnoses and limited therapies. The obesity paradox challenges conventional thinking by suggesting that individuals with obesity and certain diseases, including cancer, may have an improved prognosis compared with their counterparts of a normal weight. This observation has prompted investigations to understand protective mechanisms, including potentially favorable adipokine secretion and metabolic reserves that contribute to tolerating cancer treatments. However, understanding the association between obesity and lung cancer is complex. While smoking is the primary risk factor of lung cancer, obesity may independently impact lung cancer risk, particularly in non‑smokers. Adipose tissue dysfunction, including low‑grade chronic inflammation, and hormonal changes contribute to lung cancer development and progression. Obesity‑related factors may also influence treatment responses and survival outcomes in patients with lung cancer. The impact of obesity on treatment modalities such as chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery is still under investigation. Challenges in managing patients with obesity and cancer include increased surgical complexity, higher rates of postoperative complications and limited treatment options due to comorbidities. Targeted interventions aimed at reducing obesity prevalence and promoting healthy lifestyles are crucial for lung cancer prevention. The impact of obesity on lung cancer is multifaceted and requires further research to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and develop personalized interventions for prevention and treatment.

We need this study because some people with obesity seem to live longer with some cancers than people with normal weight, which is called the “obesity paradox” (Abstract, sentence 3). You may want to know if your weight can change your chance of lung cancer or how well treatment may work (Abstract, sentence 6). The researchers read and summed up past studies on body weight, lung cancer risk, body fat changes, and cancer care (Abstract, sentence 5). They also looked at how body fat hormones and long‑term mild swelling in the body may play a role (Abstract, sentence 7). They found that smoking is still the main cause of lung cancer, but obesity may also raise risk, mainly in people who do not smoke (Abstract, sentence 6). Changes in body fat may affect how lung cancer starts, grows, and responds to treatment, and may change surgery risk and side effects (Abstract, sentence 7). Obesity can make surgery harder and raise the chance of problems after surgery (Abstract, sentence 10). These findings suggest that healthy weight and life habits may help lower lung cancer risk (Abstract, sentence 11). More research may lead to care plans that fit a person’s weight and body needs (Abstract, sentence 12).

Title: Traditional Chinese medicine in lung cancer treatment.
Abstract: Lung cancer remains a major global health challenge and one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Despite significant advancements in treatment, challenges such as drug resistance, side effects, metastasis and recurrence continue to impact patient outcomes and quality of life. In response, there is growing interest in complementary and integrative approaches to cancer care. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with its long history, abundant clinical experience, holistic perspective and individualized approach, has garnered increasing attention for its role in lung cancer prevention and management. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the advances in TCM for lung cancer treatment, covering its theoretical foundation, treatment principles, clinical experiences and evidence supporting its efficacy. We also provide a systematic summary of the preclinical mechanisms, through which TCM impacts lung cancer, including the induction of cell death, reversal of drug resistance, inhibition of metastasis and modulation of immune responses. Additionally, future prospects for TCM in lung cancer treatment are discussed, offering insights into its expanded application and integration with modern medicine to address this challenging disease.

Title: Lung Cancer-Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Treatment and Molecular Aspect (Review of Literature).
Abstract: Lung cancer is one of the most common malignant cancers in most countries and is the leading cause of death among cancer diseases worldwide. Despite constant progress in diagnosis and therapy, survival rates of patients diagnosed with lung cancer remain unsatisfactory. Numerous epidemiological and experimental studies conducted as early as the 1970s confirm that the most important risk factor for the development of lung cancer is long-term smoking, which remains valid to this day. In the paper, the authors present the latest data on the epidemiology, pathogenesis, treatment and molecular aspects of this cancer. In the last decade, many molecular alterations that are effective in the development of lung cancer have been discovered. In adenocarcinoma, tyrosine kinase inhibitors were developed for EGFR mutations and ALK and ROS1 translocations and were approved for use in the treatment of advanced stage adenocarcinomas. In the case of squamous cell carcinoma, the evaluation of these mutations is not yet being used in clinical practice. In addition, there are ongoing studies concerning many potential therapeutic molecular targets, such as ROS, MET, FGFR, DDR-2 and RET. Constant progress in diagnostic and therapeutic methods gives rise to hopes for an improved prognosis in patients with lung cancer.

They report that, in the last ten years, many key gene changes that drive lung cancer have been found (Abstract, sentence 5). Title: Lung Cancer: Targeted Therapy in 2025.
Abstract: Lung cancer treatment has changed in the last twenty years since the discovery of EGFR mutations. In this article, we will review the current state of the art for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) actionable genomic alterations (AGA). AGAs are mostly found in lung adenocarcinomas, a subtype of non-small cell lung cancers. We will focus on the current treatment for EGFR mutations, ALK fusions, ROS1 fusions, BRAF V600E mutations, MET exon 14-skipping mutations, RET fusions, KRAS G12C mutations, ERBB2 mutations (also called HER2 mutations), and NTRK fusions. We will also touch on the key toxicities associated with these medications. Treatments are mostly available for the metastatic stage, but we will also discuss adjuvant therapy for EGFR mutations and ALK fusions, as well as stage III post-chemoradiotherapy treatment for EGFR lung cancer.

It may help people whose lung cancer has one of several known gene changes that doctors can test for (Abstract, sentence 4). The writers of this paper read and summed up many past studies on these gene changes and the drugs that target them (Abstract, sentence 2). They looked at drugs for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, KRAS, ERBB2 (HER2), and NTRK gene changes (Abstract, sentence 4). They found that most of these drugs are used when the cancer has spread, and some are now used after surgery or after chemo and radiation in certain stages (Abstract, sentence 6). They also note the main side effects of these drugs (Abstract, sentence 5). These findings may help you and your care team pick tests and drugs that best match your lung cancer type (Abstract, sentence 2).

Title: The Current Roadmap of Lung Cancer Biology, Genomics and Racial Disparity.
Abstract: Globally, lung cancer is the most prevalent cause of cancer-related death. There are two large histological groups of lung cancer: small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Based on histopathological and molecular features, adenocarcinoma (ADC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) are the two major histologic subtypes of NSCLC. Various epidemiological and environmental factors are linked with an increased risk of lung cancer. However, these risk factors show disparities in patients with divergent racial and ethnic backgrounds. Interestingly, different populations were found to harbor distinct molecular features as evidenced by variations in genetic mutation profiles. Moreover, diverse histological and molecular progression patterns are identified in lung cancer, which could be crucial in improving diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic planning. In concert with a plethora of nuclear genetic alterations, mitochondrial alteration, epigenetic reprogramming, microbial dysbiosis, and immune alteration signatures have been identified in various lung cancer types. This review article provides a comprehensive overview of screening tests and the treatment strategies for NSCLC and SCLC, including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapies. Through the unification of these diverse aspects, this review article aspires to a complete understanding of lung cancer's genomics, biology, microbial landscapes, and racial disparity and seeks to understand the essential role of racial and ethnic factors in lung cancer occurrence and treatment.

We wrote this study because many things in your life and environment can raise lung cancer risk, and these risks are not the same for all race and ethnic groups (Abstract, sentence 4).
